ceb.title: Is the New Testament Reliable?
ceb.question: Wasn't the New Testament written long after Jesus, full of legends, and corrupted through copying?
ceb.answer: The New Testament is the best-attested document of antiquity, surviving in over 5,800 Greek manuscripts, some fragments dating within a century of the originals, far exceeding the handful of late copies we have for authors like Tacitus or Caesar. The Gospels were composed within the lifetime of eyewitnesses; Paul's letters date to the 50s AD, and he appeals to over five hundred living witnesses of the risen Christ (1 Cor 15:6). Luke writes explicitly as a careful historian relying on eyewitness testimony (Lk 1:1-4). The textual variants are overwhelmingly minor spelling or word-order differences and affect no doctrine, so the message has been transmitted with remarkable fidelity. The Church that authored, preserved, and canonized these writings vouches for their apostolic origin, and their internal candor about the disciples' failures argues against legendary invention.

en.answer_full:
> "Luke's history is unsurpassed in respect of its trustworthiness. You may press the words of Luke in a degree beyond any other historian's, and they will not yield; they stand the keenest scrutiny."
> — Sir William Mitchell Ramsay, *The Bearing of Recent Discovery on the Trustworthiness of the New Testament* (1915)

The reliability of the New Testament documents is one of the most thoroughly examined questions in the humanities. Skeptics, believers, and neutral scholars have weighed the manuscript evidence, the dating of the texts, the internal consistency, and the archaeological corroboration for two centuries. The verdict of the evidence — not theological commitment — is that the New Testament is the best-attested collection of ancient documents in existence and was produced within the lifetime of people who were present at the events it describes.

---

## Textual Reliability: Manuscript Evidence

### The Numbers

The New Testament survives in over **5,800 Greek manuscripts** — more than any other ancient document by orders of magnitude. For comparison:

| Ancient Work | Manuscripts | Earliest Copy | Gap from Original |
|--------------|-------------|---------------|-------------------|
| Homer, *Iliad* | ~1,900 | c. 400 BC | ~500 years |
| Julius Caesar, *Gallic Wars* | 10 | ~900 AD | ~900 years |
| Tacitus, *Annals* | 2 | ~1100 AD | ~1,000 years |
| **New Testament** | **5,800+ Greek** | c. **AD 125** | **~25–70 years** |

The *Rylands Papyrus* (P52), a fragment of John 18, dates to approximately AD 125–150 — within 30–50 years of John's composition. The *Chester Beatty Papyri* (c. AD 250) contain large portions of the Gospels, Acts, and Paul's letters. The manuscript wealth does not introduce uncertainty — it enables *cross-checking* that reduces it.

### Textual Variants

Critics sometimes cite 400,000 "variants" in the manuscript tradition. What this means in practice: the overwhelming majority are spelling differences, transpositions, and harmless synonyms. New Testament scholar Daniel Wallace estimates that only about 400 variants (0.1%) affect the meaning of a passage in any significant way, and *no essential Christian doctrine* depends on a textually disputed passage.

---

## Dating: Written Within Living Memory

### Paul's Letters (AD 50–65)

Paul wrote 1 Corinthians approximately AD 54–55. In chapter 15:3–8, he transmits an early creedal formula:

> *"For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures; that he was buried; that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures; that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve. After that, he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep."* (1 Corinthians 15:3–5, NABRE)

Paul explicitly says he *received* this formula — meaning it predates 1 Corinthians by years. Critical scholars date this creed to within 2–5 years of the Crucifixion (c. AD 33–38). Paul met Peter personally (Galatians 1:18) and James the brother of the Lord (Galatians 1:19) — primary eyewitnesses. The resurrection claim is not a legend that developed over centuries; it appears in a formula that circulated while eyewitnesses were alive and could be questioned.

### The Gospels (AD 65–95)

Even critical scholars who deny apostolic authorship date the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) to AD 65–85 and John to AD 90–95. By ancient standards, this is strikingly early — composed within 35–65 years of the events and while eyewitnesses were still living. Luke 1:1–4 explicitly names his method: interviewing *"eyewitnesses and ministers of the word"* who handed down the tradition.

---

## Archaeological Corroboration

### The Pool of Bethesda

John 5:2 describes a pool near the Sheep Gate with *five porticoes* where Jesus healed a paralyzed man. For centuries this description was considered improbable. Excavations in Jerusalem in the 1950s revealed a pool matching John's description exactly — including the five porticoes that had puzzled skeptics, explained by a wall dividing two adjacent pools. John's local topographical knowledge is consistently precise.

### The Ossuary of Caiaphas

In 1990, a burial cave in Jerusalem yielded an ossuary (bone box) inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas" — almost certainly the High Priest who presided at Jesus's trial (Matthew 26:57). An ossuary of this individual's existence and name being confirmed independently corroborates the New Testament's historical setting.

### Pilate Inscription (Caesarea Maritima, 1961)

A limestone block discovered at Caesarea Maritima bears the inscription: *"[Pon]tius Pilatus / [Praef]ectus Iuda[eae]"* — confirming both the existence and the title of the Roman official who condemned Jesus.

### Synagogues at Capernaum and Chorazin

The Gospels repeatedly locate Jesus's ministry at Capernaum (Matthew 4:13, John 6:59) and surrounding towns. Excavations at Capernaum confirmed a synagogue at the site — directly beneath the 4th-century synagogue visible today is earlier black basalt construction consistent with a 1st-century synagogue.

---

## Internal Evidence: Hallmarks of Eyewitness Testimony

Psychologists and historians of eyewitness testimony identify certain features that distinguish firsthand accounts from later legends:

1. **Embarrassing details** — The Gospels record that the disciples *fled* at the arrest (Mark 14:50), Peter *denied* Christ three times (Mark 14:66–72), and the first resurrection witnesses were *women* (whose testimony was not legally admissible under Roman law — Luke 24:10–11). Invented accounts do not include details damaging to the heroes.

2. **Unresolved tensions** — The four Gospels have minor differences in details (number of angels at the tomb, exact sequence of resurrection appearances). These variations reflect multiple independent witnesses remembering the same events slightly differently — not editorial coordination. Fabricated documents harmonize their details; eyewitness accounts do not.

3. **Accurate local color** — John's Gospel uses precise Jerusalem topographical terms (*Gabbatha*, *Golgotha*, named pools and gates) that match later archaeological discovery. This degree of local accuracy is not characteristic of legend but of a text produced by someone with direct knowledge of the city.

---

## External Corroboration

### Tacitus (c. AD 117)

Roman historian Tacitus, in *Annals* XV.44, describing Nero's persecution of Christians:

> *"Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus."*

Tacitus, hostile to Christianity, confirms: Jesus existed, died under Pilate, and his movement persisted despite the execution.

### Josephus (c. AD 93)

Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian, refers to *"James the brother of Jesus who was called Christ"* (*Antiquities*, XX.9.1) and in the *Testimonium Flavianum* (*Antiquities*, XVIII.3.3) provides a description of Jesus's ministry and death — though this passage has likely been partially interpolated by later Christian copyists, the core references are widely accepted as authentic.

---

## Common Objections

**"The Gospels were written decades after the events — they are legends, not history."**

Decades is not centuries. The Gospels were written 35–65 years after the Crucifixion — while eyewitnesses were still alive. By the standards applied to other ancient texts (Tacitus, Plutarch, Josephus), this is excellent proximity. The early creedal material in 1 Corinthians 15 dates to within years of the events.

**"The Gospels contradict each other — they can't be reliable."**

Minor variations in detail (how many women at the tomb, the sequence of appearances) reflect independent eyewitness accounts, not fabrication. Courts regularly receive multiple eyewitness testimonies that agree on the central facts but differ on peripheral details; the differences are taken as evidence of authenticity, not fabrication. The core claims — death by crucifixion, empty tomb, resurrection appearances — are consistent across all four Gospels.

**"The Catholic Church chose which books to include — the Bible is a human construct."**

The Church did not invent the canon — she recognized books already in widespread use among the apostolic communities. The process was one of discernment and formal recognition, not arbitrary selection. The criteria were apostolic origin, consistent liturgical use, and doctrinal coherence with the received faith. Books excluded (like the Gnostic gospels) were written in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, long after the apostolic generation — they are the late-comer forgeries, not the canonical texts.

---

The New Testament is not a document of blind faith. It is the most thoroughly corroborated, earliest-attested, and best-preserved body of texts from the ancient world. Its historical framework is confirmed by archaeology, Roman historians, and Jewish sources. Its manuscript tradition is unparalleled in depth and consistency. The Catholic claim rests not on credulous acceptance of legend but on engagement with some of the most compelling historical evidence the ancient world has left us.
